headline: Unloved parts of the market offer compelling opportunities; favour solid income, low CapEx risk, high-quality assets in good locations
reasoning: Abell argues that the parts of the market that are 'unloved' are where compelling opportunities currently exist. He draws a contrast with 2021 when there were many reasons to buy and those who sold then positioned themselves well for the next phase of the cycle. The investment criteria he is currently focused on are a solid income backbone, limited capital expenditure risk, and high-quality assets in good locations as a hedge if rental growth becomes harder to come by.
quote: we think some of the parts of the market that probably a little bit unloved, you know, there's sometimes you look at things and there's, there's almost no reason to buy these things. Whereas at the top of the market there's lots of reasons to buy things. And that's how a cycle plays out. And certainly in 2021 there was lots of reasons to buy real estate and those were brave enough and we certainly sold quite a few assets in 2021 that they were the ones that really positioned themselves for the next phase of the cycle. So in terms of what we're looking for, we're looking for a solid income backbone, not a lot of CapEx risk and just high quality assets in good locations.
episode_title: Finding value amid the property reset

headline: Offshore investors hit by absentee owner charges in Queensland and Victoria; negative impact now priced into the market
reasoning: Abell highlights that offshore property investors have faced additional costs over the last couple of years through absentee owner surcharges in Queensland and Victoria, which have tarnished returns. However, he notes these factors are now priced into the market, which is why the current entry point looks attractive — the downside is already reflected in valuations.
quote: Certainly offshore investors have been hit with that as well over the last couple of years with some big absentee owner charges in Queensland as well as in Victoria, which is really some tarnished some returns in there. But you know, when we look at those components of the income now, they're priced into the market and that's where it looks really interesting to us that these downside factors are priced.
episode_title: Finding value amid the property reset

headline: Cautious on development for some time; very hard to make a dollar in development even now, preferring well-built high-quality existing assets
reasoning: Abell explains that development can produce fantastic returns in rising markets but is highly sensitive to cost price inflation, falling values, pre-sales collapsing, tenant failures at completion, and planning challenges. The developer model — land plus construction plus interest plus holding costs plus margin — has many moving parts that can turn against you quickly. He says his firm has been very cautious on development for quite some time and even now sees it as very hard to make a dollar, preferring to earn returns from high-quality existing assets.
quote: Well, development can be a very glamorous place to be and there can be some fantastic returns to be made in development, particularly in rising markets. But when things go wrong, whether that's cost price inflation, whether it's in values going down, whether it's pre sales falling over, whether it might be your tenant falling over in a commercial building, for example, they might have some struggles within their business. They might not be able to occupy your new building at completion. There's many different where it could be planning changes, planning challenges. There's many challenges to being a developer. And ultimately their model is relatively simple. It's they take a cost base being land, construction costs, interest costs, holding costs and then add a margin and hopefully that's above the valuation that they'll get or the sales price that they get at the end of the day. And all these factors are sensitive and when they move against you, it can be really quite painful. So we've been really quite cautious on development for quite some time. And even now it seems very hard to make a dollar in development. So we're very happy earning well built high quality assets.
episode_title: Finding value amid the property reset

headline: Excited to deploy into the next part of the cycle; 10% through-the-cycle return target with medium-to-long-term horizon required to weather bumps
reasoning: Abell notes that the fund returned just over 10% in the last 12 months and has averaged 9.3% over the last 10 years. He frames 10% as a good through-the-cycle return target but cautions investors need a medium-to-long-term view because there will be bumps along the way. The fund has not missed a regular distribution in over 20 years, which he attributes to the quality of assets and disciplined capital management including not taking on too much debt at any given point in the cycle.
quote: Our fund hasn't missed a regular distribution in over 20 years. And that's partially a function of the assets that we own, but also our approach to Capital Management and not having too much debt at any given point in time in the cycle. So over the last 10 years, our average return has been 9.3%. As I said earlier, in the last 12 months it's been 10.8%. And so, you know, we feel as though 10% through the cycle. It's a good way to look at your return, but you need to have a view towards the medium to long term because along the way there'll be bumps.
episode_title: Finding value amid the property reset

headline: Secondary assets and macro-exposed tenants at risk; liquidity tight in private equity real estate but abundant in private credit
reasoning: Abell warns that investors holding secondary assets should be concerned about their income profile and ability to sell. Private equity real estate liquidity is currently tight, contrasting with the boom period. Assets tenanted by businesses exposed to the tough macro environment are particularly vulnerable, with several occupiers in the industrial space having recently fallen over. He cites a large distribution and freight company needing $180 million by the start of next year as an example of broader macro stress.
quote: certainly if I was owning secondary assets, I'd be somewhat concerned about the income profile and being able to sell those assets and equally those those assets that are tenanted by buildings that are somewhat exposed to the tougher macro environment that we're in right now. And we've seen a number of occupiers fall over in the industrial space recently. And and it was only a couple of days ago, a very large distribution freight moving company was out there in the market stating that they need $180 million by the start of next year to keep going in their business.
episode_title: Finding value amid the property reset

headline: Interest rates were the primary driver of both the COVID-era valuation runup and subsequent write-downs; downside factors now priced into the market
reasoning: Abell argues the unwinding of property valuations was primarily driven by interest rates, just as the write-up during COVID was largely rate-driven. He views the COVID period as an aberration that has now washed through the market. With those negative factors — including rising rates and absentee owner charges in Queensland and Victoria — now priced in, he sees greater upside available for investors entering at current levels.
quote: I think certainly the unwinding of valuations was driven by interest rates and equally the write up was largely driven by interest rates and particularly during that COVID. Which was really an aberration in terms of asset values. You know, when we look at the market historically, we basically take out that period of the market and go back to what the cycle was prior to COVID hitting and it was at the top. So you know, we've now seen that washed through. And if you look back to where asset values were now, depending on what part of the market you're looking at, they might be back to 2018 levels, they might be back to 2012 levels.
episode_title: Finding value amid the property reset

headline: Active tenant management — running buildings efficiently, understanding tenant needs, facilitating expansions — creates significant value through the cycle independent of market rental growth
reasoning: Abell illustrates that active management can create material value even when rental growth is elusive. Simple measures like improving cleaning, car parking and tenant communication improve retention and rental outcomes. A live example involves working with a growing tenant who needs more space in 12–24 months, while placing a short-term tenant in that space now to bridge the gap — allowing the larger tenant to expand without cash-flow risk to the landlord.
quote: it can be really significant and it can might be as as simple as just running your building more efficiently and being attentive to your tenants. So for example, we've we bought a building back in May and we've been in there speaking with the tenants regularly. Their prior landlord didn't speak to them a lot... And equally you can help them expand their business or shrink their business without taking a lot of cash flow risk on yourself. So you know, live case in case in point that we have, we're working with a live tenant at the moment. Their business is growing. It's not ready to take on more space for probably another 12 to 24 months, so we're now working with another tenant who will take space for short term to allow us to allow our larger tenant to grow even more.
episode_title: Finding value amid the property reset

headline: Property market entering a new cycle after four years of tight liquidity and significant repricing; asset values in some segments back to 2012-2018 levels
reasoning: Abell notes that liquidity has been very tight for four years and investors have been cautious. The COVID period created an aberration in asset values that has now largely washed through. Depending on the sub-sector, asset values are now back to 2018 or even 2012 levels, though rent inflation and development cost changes mean it is not a direct like-for-like comparison. He sees this repricing as creating an attractive entry point for the next part of the cycle.
quote: Well, I think they've been cautious for about four years now. Liquidity's been really tight for four years and liquidity's gone elsewhere. But in certainly in 2000 and 2021, liquidity was, the market was awash with liquidity and that was after a really long cycle anyway leading up from 2010. So investors have been cautious and there's been some really hard times out there for a number of investors potentially invested in, assets that have either had tenants that have fallen over, they've repriced because they were just overpriced to start with, particularly during that sort of COVID froth where asset values really got beat up significantly. And those investors who were brave enough to sell at the top of the market are now feeling really good and looking forward to deploying into this next part of the cycle, which is certainly where we're excited to be deploying.
episode_title: Finding value amid the property reset
